newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bezeq Telecom faces an uncertain future.
newsitem.headline: Bezeq Telecom faces an uncertain future.

text.p: Bezeq Israel Telecom, Israel's main telecommunications carrier, faces an uncertain future as the company enters an era of heightened competition and its chief executive prepares to leave, analysts said on Thursday.

The concerns about Bezeq have been reflected in the company's Tel Aviv share price. Since the beginning of November, Bezeq has risen less than nine percent to a Wednesday close of 8.65 shekels ($2.61), while the Mishtanim index of top 100 shares has soared 30 percent.

"It's a good company. I just think that as long as there isn't growth in earnings, there won't be massive growth in the share price," said Keith Phillips of Societe Generale Equities & Derivatives in London.
The company is 76 percent-owned by the Israeli government, which plans to reduce its stake to 51 percent with a global offering.
Bezeq's monopoly over telephone service has been whittled down over the last five years, but under its widely admired managing director Yitzhak Kaul the company turned itself into nimble competitor.
Kaul trimmed Bezeq's workforce to some 8,500 from a peak of 10,300 in 1992, forced equipment suppliers to cut prices and invested heavily in upgrading its network.

"Kaul was someone unusual. But when you're speaking about a company the size of Bezeq...good management cannot be just a good CEO. It has to be something wider than this," said Boaz Leviatan of Sahar Securities, a Tel Aviv broker.

Kaul's successor, Yoram Turbowicz, previously head of the government's anti-trust authority, is untested. Analysts said his strengths were in understanding competitive issues and his good government contacts.
Turbowicz has his work cut out. Later this year Bezeq will face competition in its hugely profitable international phone service business.

The government has awarded licences to two international consortiums to offer competing service. They bid at tariff rates a fraction of what Bezeq now charges and will force the company to drop its rates accordingly, Phillips said.
"The problem is that no one knows what the impact will be. On the one hand, prices will drop," Leviatan said. "On the other, international traffic over the Bezeq network will increase."
Bezeq also faces more competition in its cellular business as the government plans to publish a tender for a third operator by July.

Further down the line, the government aims to open basic and interurban telephone service as well as telecommunications infrastructure to competition by the end of 1998. However, analysts said damage from that competition would be limited.

"What the net effect of these (competitive) measures will be is still unclear but we believe that earnings growth will be halted as early as 1997," said a Societe Generale report on Bezeq published in November. Earnings per share could drop by 16 percent in 1998, it said.
Analysts said the market would still welcome the government's share offering provided issues of ownership and control are sorted out.

Cable & Wireless Plc bought 10 percent of Bezeq in the stock market two years ago, to the government's chagrin. Now the two sides are in talks over what the British company's role will be. Cable & Wireless has hinted it wants to become the main shareholder in Bezeq, but analysts said the government and management would prefer another company.
